# Archaeology of North Korea

The archaeological record of what is now North Korea stretches from the first human presence in the peninsula during the Middle Pleistocene to the medieval Goryeo period. The Korean peninsula contains abundant evidence of human habitation across multiple prehistoric and historic periods, including distinctive pottery traditions, monumental stone structures known as dolmens, and richly decorated royal tombs. Modern North Korean archaeology is characterized by distinctive methodological approaches derived from Juche ideology, which emphasizes Korean cultural independence and development, and incorporates elements of Marxist historiography. This ideological framework influences interpretations of the archaeological record and diverges from scholarly practices in other regions.

# Archaeological Record

### Paleolithic Period

The earliest human presence in the Korean peninsula dates to the Early Paleolithic, though the precise chronology remains disputed. Objects resembling stone tools have been found at Hukwuri Cave, part of the Komun Moru site in Sangwon County southeast of Pyongyang, though questions persist regarding their dating and human attribution. While disputed Homo erectus remains have been found in South Korea, they are well attested in northeastern China, suggesting human presence in Korea likely dates to the Middle Pleistocene. Homo erectus likely dispersed throughout the peninsula after entering from Northern China via the coastal plains.

Claims of Neanderthal sites dating to the Riss-Würm interglacial period (approximately 120,000 years ago) have been made for both North and South Korea, but without conclusive supporting evidence. Later specimens from the Last Glacial Period have been designated as Homo sapiens. The paleolithic inhabitants of Korea subsisted through hunting of wild boar and deer, fishing, and foraging, though the absence of projectile points and storage containers in the archaeological record makes identifying specific foods consumed difficult. Climate conditions during the Pleistocene remained relatively mild and stable within the peninsula, though rising sea levels during interglacial periods flooded vast coastal plains and restricted inhabitants to mountainous and forested interior regions.

In Korean archaeological chronology, the period from approximately 15,000 to 8,000 BCE is termed the Terminal Paleolithic. The peninsula's population remained dispersed into small hunter-gatherer groups; one scholarly study suggested a total population of no more than 40,000 during the last two millennia of the Paleolithic.

### Jeulmun Pottery Period (c. 8000–1500 BCE)

The Jeulmun pottery period represents the Mesolithic and Neolithic cultural stages in Korea. The period is named after the decorated pottery vessels—juman (즐문) meaning "comb-patterned"—that form a large part of the pottery assemblage. The earliest Jeulmun pottery, termed Yunggimun or raised-design pottery, dates to approximately 5,000 BCE and is characterized by flat-bottomed wares with relief designs and raised horizontal lines. The Early Jeulmun period (c. 6000–3500 BCE) is characterized by deep-sea fishing, hunting, and small semi-permanent settlements with pit-houses. Samples from settlements such as Seopohang, Amsa-dong, and Osan-ri demonstrate evidence of sedentary occupation.

In North Korea, prominent Jeulmun sites include Chitamni on the Chaeryong River, noted for the presence of grain remains, and Chonghori just east of Pyongyang, which contains both Jeulmun and Yunggimun pottery. A cluster of sites found along the Yalu River exhibits distinctions from classical Jeulmun pottery, while another cluster around the Tumen River, on the borders with China and Russia, shows stronger affiliation with Neolithic cultures of southeastern Siberia.

### Mumun Period (c. 1500–300 BCE)

The Mumun pottery period, named for undecorated or plain cooking and storage vessels, spans approximately 1500 to 300 BCE. The Mumun culture, likely spreading into the peninsula from northeast China around the second millennium BCE, is attested by megalithic dolmens and large villages of pit-houses. This period saw the introduction of bronze-working technology and the establishment of fully agricultural subsistence patterns. The Early Mumun period (c. 1500–850 BCE) is characterized by shifting cultivation, fishing, hunting, and discrete settlements with rectangular semi-subterranean pit-houses, predominantly located in river valleys of west-central Korea. By the end of this sub-period, larger settlements began appearing, and long-standing traditions related to Mumun ceremonial and mortuary systems, including megalithic burials and red-burnished pottery production, took shape.

Dolmens (Korean: goindol, literally "propped stone"), which serve as burial sites representative of the Bronze Age, are found throughout the Korean peninsula in high concentrations. Approximately 30,000 dolmens have been identified in South Korea and between 10,000 and 15,000 in North Korea, together accounting for over 40 percent of all dolmens identified worldwide. Dolmens take two main forms: "table" dolmens constructed with upright stone slabs surrounding an above-ground burial cist and a flat capstone roof, and "checkerboard" dolmens featuring underground burial chambers made with piled stone fragments covered by a capstone. The considerable labor required to move massive capstones—estimated at 200 workers needed for a 32-ton stone—suggests that table dolmen construction required concentrated social organization and power.

Burial offerings including earthenware, stone tools, and bronze wares recovered from dolmens provide insights into Bronze Age society and economy.

### Wiman Joseon and Lelang Commandery Period (109 BCE–313 CE)

Wiman Joseon, an ancient Korean kingdom that emerged in the area around modern Pyongyang, was conquered by the Chinese Han dynasty in 109 BCE. Following this conquest, the Han established the Lelang Commandery as part of the Four Commanderies of Han. The Lelang Commandery dominated portions of North Korea for approximately 400 years, though it left relatively few archaeological remains. Tombs and burial mounds constitute the most common archaeological sites from the Lelang period. Some dates can be determined from Lelang artifacts; for example, a lacquer bowl recovered from Lelang contexts is dated by inscription to 69 CE.

The interpretation of Lelang Commandery archaeological remains has become contested within North Korean scholarship, which reinterprets artifacts such as tombs, jewelry, and lacquerware as remains of Gojoseon or Goguryeo rather than Han colonial sites, reflecting Juche-influenced scholarly perspectives.

### Goguryeo Period (37 BCE–668 CE)

Goguryeo, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, developed a distinct material culture incorporating influences from both China and nomadic groups of the northwest. The kingdom, traditionally dated to a foundation around 37 BCE, eventually established its capital at Pyongyang in 427 CE. Royal tombs initially took the form of pyramidal structures constructed from cut stone, while later examples consist of hemispherical tumuli containing stone burial chambers. Although nearly all were plundered in antiquity, many tombs still contain elaborate murals.

Archaeological evidence from Goguryeo sites includes horse equipment and some of the earliest known examples of stirrups. Over 10,000 Goguryeo tombs of various types exist throughout the region, with approximately 90 unearthed in China and Korea containing preserved wall paintings. These murals depict scenes of daily life, religious practices, warfare, and mythology, offering invaluable insights into Goguryeo society. The murals show vivid coloration and are concentrated in several regions, with approximately 70 murals documented primarily in the Taedong river basin near Pyongyang, the Anak area in South Hwanghae province, and in Ji'an in China's Jilin province.

The Anak Tomb No. 3, discovered near Pyongyang in 1949, ranks among the most significant Goguryeo monuments. Constructed from basalt and limestone blocks, the tomb's internal configuration consists of an entryway, foreroom, antechamber with side-rooms, and burial chamber aligned on a south-north axis. The tomb's wall paintings are particularly important for understanding the development of Goguryeo mural traditions. Inscriptions within the tomb allow dating to approximately 357 CE, during the reign of King Gogukwon. The site was excavated immediately following Korean independence with the intention of preserving cultural heritage, and continuous investigation and study have continued since the first formal report in 1958.

### Unified Silla and Balhae Periods (668–926 CE)

Following the conquest of Baekje in 660 and Goguryeo in 668 by Silla with Tang Dynasty assistance, the Unified Silla kingdom controlled most of the peninsula. The northern region of the defeated Goguryeo later reemerged as Balhae (698–926 CE), which ruled Manchuria and northern Korean territories. Both kingdoms eventually fell to the emerging Goryeo state by 935 CE. Archaeological evidence from these periods indicates advanced material culture, with Buddhism and aristocratic society forming the twin pillars of Unified Silla civilization. The period from 668 to 926 is sometimes termed the "North-South States period" (nambukguk sidae) by historians, reflecting the simultaneous rule of these two polities.

### Goryeo Period (918–1392 CE)

Goryeo, which succeeded Balhae and eventually unified the peninsula, developed distinctive ceramic traditions that form important components of the archaeological record. Goryeo ceramic production was initially influenced by Yuezhou kilns from southern China but later integrated elements from northern China, including concurrent production of celadon and white porcelain, unique vessel forms, and decoration techniques such as inlaying and iron-painting. These innovations were influenced by interactions with the Liao and Jin dynasties. The influence of northern China introduced technological advances such as secondary firing and new vessel designs, creating a fusion of diverse cultural influences in Goryeo ceramic evolution.

# Methodological Approaches and Institutional Framework

### North Korean Archaeological Practice

The development of archaeology in North Korea followed a distinctive trajectory shaped by political ideology and institutional factors. Initial academic practice in early North Korea drew heavily from Soviet models, which emphasized Marxist interpretive frameworks. Among the first major archaeological discoveries of the newly independent North Korean state were the excavation of a shell midden in Unggi County in 1947 and the discovery of three Goguryeo tombs, including the richly decorated Anak Tomb No. 3, near Pyongyang in 1949. Initial findings were published in the ethnographic journal Munhwa yumul (Cultural Properties), which appeared from 1949 to 1950, with subsequent work appearing in various historical journals.

Archaeological excavations resumed in 1954 following the Korean War armistice, with early work aimed at documenting and restoring cultural heritage damaged during the conflict. During the 1950s, North Korean archaeologists under leadership (notably the archaeologist To) conducted excavations at important sites including the Bronze Age Odong site in Hoeryong (1954–1955) and the Neolithic Jitapri site in Pongsan (1957).

### Juche Ideology and Historiography

Modern North Korean archaeology is oriented around Juche ideology, which incorporates elements of nationalism and Marxist historiography. This framework reflects the broader political emphasis on Korean independence and self-reliance and is reflected in archaeological interpretation and chronology. The Juche perspective presents Korean civilization as having developed independently, explicitly rejecting interpretations that emphasize Chinese influence on Korean cultural development. This ideological orientation influences methodological choices and chronological assignments.

North Korean archaeologists demonstrate a preference for using traditional historical accounts in lieu of radiocarbon dating, resulting in a less conservative chronology than that adopted by South Korean counterparts, who rely more extensively on scientific dating techniques. A notable example involves the interpretation of Paleolithic remains; North Korean scholars employ different methodological approaches, utilizing object typology and stratigraphy rather than the radiocarbon dating preferred in international practice, which leads to notably earlier dating of archaeological evidence. In the mid-1960s, following ideological shifts emphasizing Juche principles, North Korean archaeologists reported discovery of Paleolithic cultural remains, reflecting the empowerment of archaeological research through alignment with state ideology.

The divergence between North and South Korean archaeological methodologies results in significant differences in chronological assignments for the same periods and sites. This distinction reflects both methodological preference and the broader ideological framework within which North Korean scholarship operates.

### Research Institutions

The Institute of Archaeology of the Academy of Social Sciences and the Faculty of History at Kim Il Sung University serve as the primary archaeological organizations in North Korea. These institutions offer archaeological degree programs, publish academic journals, and conduct archaeological excavations throughout the country. The Faculty of History at Kim Il Sung University maintains educational and research missions focused on training specialists in historical study and conducting original research.

The earliest human presence in the [Korean peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_peninsula "Korean peninsula") date to the [Early Paleolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Paleolithic "Early Paleolithic"). The precise dating of the earliest archaic humans is uncertain, with several sites of disputed age or human presence. Objects resembling [stone tools](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stone_tool "Stone tool") have been found at Hukwuri Cave (흑우리 동굴), part of the [Komun Moru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Komun_Moru "Komun Moru") site in [Sangwon County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sangwon_County "Sangwon County"), southeast of the North Korean capital of [Pyongyang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pyongyang "Pyongyang"). Hand-axes similar to the [Acheulean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acheulean "Acheulean") type have been found there, and at [Jeongok-ri](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeongok-ri&action=edit&redlink=1 "Jeongok-ri (page does not exist)"), just south of the [Demilitarized Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Demilitarized_Zone "Korean Demilitarized Zone") dividing North and South Korea.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBae2017223%E2%80%93224,_227%E2%80%93229-1) Found among the remains of [Middle Pleistocene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Pleistocene "Middle Pleistocene") animals and deposited at least 400,000 years ago, it is uncertain whether the objects were actually shaped by humans. While disputed _[Homo erectus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus "Homo erectus")_ remains have been found in South Korea, they are well attested in [northeastern China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeastern_China "Northeastern China"); as such, human presence in Korea likely dates to the Middle Pleistocene. _H. erectus_ likely dispersed throughout the peninsula after entering from Northern China via the coastal plains.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBae2017223%E2%80%93224,_227%E2%80%93229-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson199330,_34,_36-2) Claimed [Neanderthal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neanderthal "Neanderthal") sites dating to the [Riss-Würm interglacial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riss-W%C3%BCrm_interglacial "Riss-Würm interglacial") (c. 120,000 years ago) have been found in both North and South Korea, but without conclusive evidence. Later specimens from the [Last Glacial Period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Glacial_Period "Last Glacial Period") have been designated as _Homo sapiens_.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson199343-3)

During the [Late Paleolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Paleolithic "Late Paleolithic"), [blades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blade_/(archaeology/) "Blade (archaeology)") developed in the Korean peninsula. Stone blades likely spread to Korea somewhere between 40,000 and 30,000 years ago, possibly originating in the [Altai Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altai_Mountains "Altai Mountains") of Central Asia.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson199347-4)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBae2017229%E2%80%93235-5) At least four different stone tool industries coexisted in Korea during the Late Paleolithic. This may have been due to multiple waves of migration by different groups, including a group of blade-using peoples from Mongolia and northern China.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBae2017229%E2%80%93235-5) The paleolithic inhabitants of Korea subsisted off hunting (likely of wild boar and deer), fishing, and foraging, although a lack of [projectile points](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projectile_point "Projectile point") and storage containers within the archaeological record impedes the identification of the specific foods consumed. Climate conditions were relatively mild and stable in the peninsula during the Pleistocene, although rising sea levels during interglacial periods flooded the vast coastal plains and restricted the inhabitants to the mountainous and forested interior.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson199355%E2%80%9357-6)

In Korean archaeological chronology, the period from about 15,000 to 8,000 BCE has been termed the [Terminal Paleolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Terminal_Paleolithic&action=edit&redlink=1 "Terminal Paleolithic (page does not exist)").[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee2017452-7) The population of the peninsula was still dispersed into small hunter gatherer groups; one 2009 study suggested a total population of no more than 40,000 during the last two millennia of the Paleolithic.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee2017467-8) [Microblade technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microblade_technology "Microblade technology") entered the peninsula shortly before the Terminal Paleolithic from Mongolia, but other microblade traditions possibly originated in Japan.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBae2017229%E2%80%93235-5) This period was marked by an almost complete lack of sites in the archaeological record until the late 20th century, and some previous models suggested that Korea was abandoned during this period. Although discoveries in the late 20th century narrowed this relatively unattested time period,[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson199347%E2%80%9353-9) there remains very few known sites until the introduction of pottery some millennia later.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBae2017229%E2%80%93235-5)

The [Neolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic "Neolithic") in the Korean peninsula corresponds to the [Jeulmun period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeulmun_pottery_period "Jeulmun pottery period"), named for a local tradition of combed pottery. The Neolithic saw the introduction of pottery, [sedentism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sedentism "Sedentism"), and likely plant cultivation.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee2017451-10) A few Korean sites have been labeled "Pre-Pottery Neolithic" due to settlement locations and stone tools more closely resembling those associated with the Neolithic.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee2017456-11) However, the namesake pottery was not the first form of ceramic in the region, and the "Jeulmun period" label is often applied to sites predating the emergence of the Jeulmun pottery itself.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson199358%E2%80%9359-12) Hunting, fishing, and foraging remained important food sources while agriculture gradually gained prominence; it is unclear when the transition to a largely agrarian society took place.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson1993103-13)

Pottery emerged in the Korean peninsula around 6000 BCE. During the early stages of the Neolithic, the dominant pottery culture of northern Korea, the [Ossani pottery](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ossani_pottery&action=edit&redlink=1 "Ossani pottery (page does not exist)"), was characterized by similarities to the [Boisman culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Boisman_culture&action=edit&redlink=1 "Boisman culture (page does not exist)") ([fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_de_Bo%C3%AFsman "fr:Culture de Boïsman")). Ossani type sites also include a wide variety of lithics, including fishhooks, axes, arrowheads, sickles, knives, pestles, and hammers. They were contemporary to the [Yunggimun pottery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yunggimun_pottery "Yunggimun pottery") type of the southeastern coast.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee2017459,_466-14) The Jeulmun pottery culture emerged on the northwestern coastal lowlands, with the oldest clusters of sites around the [Taedong River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taedong_River "Taedong River") of North Korea and the [Han River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_River_/(Korea/) "Han River (Korea)") in South Korea.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson199379-15)

Prominent Jeulmun sites in North Korea include the [Chitamni](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chitamni&action=edit&redlink=1 "Chitamni (page does not exist)") on the [Chaeryong River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaeryong_River "Chaeryong River") (noted for the presence of grains) and [Chonghori](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Chonghori&action=edit&redlink=1 "Chonghori (page does not exist)") just east of Pyongyang (noted for the presence of both Jeulmun and Yunggimun pottery). A cluster of sites have been found along the [Yalu River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yalu_River "Yalu River"), featuring a number of distinctions from the classical Jeulmun pottery, while another cluster around the [Tumen River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tumen_River "Tumen River") (on the border with China and Russia) shows a stronger affiliation with the Neolithic cultures elsewhere in southeastern Siberia.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson199384%E2%80%9388-16)

A slight majority of Jeulmun sites are [shell middens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shell_midden "Shell midden"), found along the coast or on islands. Pit-houses first appear in the archaeological record around 5500 BCE, but are rare prior to 3500. Early pit-houses have been found in the central regions of Korea, generally found in clusters of less than ten houses in sites around the Taedong, Han, and [Imjin Rivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imjin_River "Imjin River"). Around the Han and Imjin, settlements increased in size as the Neolithic progressed, generally comprising ten to twenty houses (although settlement sites larger and smaller than this are both attested). Many are located on hilltops and feature kilns.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee2017467%E2%80%93469-17) Ornamental artifacts are rarely found in Jeulmun sites, beyond scant pieces of jewelry and some clay figurines.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson1993106-18) The Jeulmun period ended around 1100.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelsonNeu2017603%E2%80%93604-19)

The [Mumun period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumun_pottery_period "Mumun pottery period") is named for the characteristic Mumun (무문; 無文; 'without markings') pottery which appeared in Korea at some point between 2300 and 1300 BCE, overlapping significantly with the Jeulmun; this may have been due to a prolonged spread of the culture into the peninsula from Northeastern China. The period saw the introduction of bronze smelting, the construction of megalithic [dolmens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolmen "Dolmen"),[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelsonNeu2017603%E2%80%93604-19) and the predominance of agriculture for subsistence.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelsonNeu2017605-20)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson1993144-21) The period's chronology is divided into early (before c. 850), middle (c. 850 – c. 550) and late (c. 550 – c. 300) stages.

Mumun village sites were larger than their Jeulmun counterparts, and gradually increased in size over the course of the period.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelsonNeu2017604-22)[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson1993139-23) Mumun villages consisted of larger pit-houses, of both circular and rectangular shape, which often contained multiple hearths. Excavated villages range from tens to hundreds of pit houses in size; among the larger village sites in North Korea are [Simchalli](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Simchalli&action=edit&redlink=1 "Simchalli (page does not exist)") and [Soktalli](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Soktalli&action=edit&redlink=1 "Soktalli (page does not exist)"), both in the [Hwanghae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hwanghae_Province "Hwanghae Province") region.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson1993139-23) Villages moved from the river valleys to the hilltops, and as such Jeulmun and Mumun artifacts are rarely found together. Settlements became less dense in the mountainous northern and eastern regions of Korea, but more favorable conditions for cultivation led to increased density in the west.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson1993138-24)

[Liaoning bronze daggers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liaoning_bronze_dagger_culture "Liaoning bronze dagger culture") feature wide protuberances from either side of the blade.

Dolmens in North Korea are similar to those found in the Liaodong Peninsula, featuring a large capstone placed atop a number of smaller slabs below. However, unlike their counterparts in Liaodong, they consist of rough, unpolished stones. Capstone dolmen are common in North Korea, but very few are found south of [Seoul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seoul "Seoul").[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelsonNeu2017604-22) Dolmen clusters are usually located near village sites,[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson1993138-24) and are thought to serve as grave markers; however, their prominence has led most to be looted, and only a few dolmen sites have produced useful archaeological remains.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelsonNeu2017604-22)

Mirrors are the most common bronze artifacts from the Mumun period,[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson1993137-25) but weapons such as daggers, spearpoints, and arrowheads are also found. The [Liaoning bronze daggers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liaoning_bronze_dagger_culture "Liaoning bronze dagger culture"), featuring wide violin-shaped protuberances, are found across much of the Korean peninsula in addition to the Liaodong Peninsula and the [Bohai Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bohai_Bay "Bohai Bay") coast.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson1993133-26) Locally produced bronze artifacts contain a greater percentage of zinc than their Chinese counterparts, with a zinc content between seven and thirteen percent. Zinc, copper, and tin are all found in the peninsula, allowing for locally available raw materials for bronze production.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson1993138-24)

By 400 BCE, innovations such as iron tools and above-ground houses spread throughout the Korean Peninsula. Although different Korean archaeologists have historically given dramatically different dates for domestic iron production (ranging from the 6th to 1st centuries BCE), it likely spread from China during the [Warring States period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Warring_States_period "Warring States period") (475–221 BCE). Trade from the state of [Yan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yan_/(state/) "Yan (state)") is attested in northwestern Korea during this period, evidenced by the presence of Yan [knife money](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knife_money "Knife money") at sites also containing iron tools.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson1993172-27) The [Musan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musan_County "Musan County") site along the Tumen River in [North Hamgyong Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Hamgyong_Province "North Hamgyong Province") show evidence of early domestic iron manufacturing (possibly dating to 480 BCE), as do various other village sites in Hwanghae and two near [Wonsan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wonsan "Wonsan") in northern [Kangwon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kangwon_Province,_North_Korea "Kangwon Province, North Korea").[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson1993174-28) Pit graves are found across Korea during this time period, with the greatest number in the northwest.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson1993183%E2%80%93184-29) Ceramics during the period differ sharply from Mumun pottery.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson1993179-30)

Chinese sources such as the _[Classic of Mountains and Seas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classic_of_Mountains_and_Seas "Classic of Mountains and Seas")_ and the [_Strategies of the Warring States_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhan_Guo_Ce "Zhan Guo Ce") briefly mention the existence of a Koren state called Joseon (now referred to as [Gojoseon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn "Old Chosŏn"), 'Old Joseon') with an unclear location; it may have been outside the Korean peninsula. The late 3rd century CE _[Records of the Three Kingdoms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Records_of_the_Three_Kingdoms "Records of the Three Kingdoms")_ describes a Chinese general named [Wiman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiman_of_Gojoseon "Wiman of Gojoseon") adopting Korean customs and founding the state of [Wiman Joseon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiman_Chos%C5%8Fn "Wiman Chosŏn") with a group of followers in the early 2nd century BCE, driving out the local ruler and establishing his capital near what is now Pyongyang. In 109 BCE, the Chinese [Han dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_dynasty "Han dynasty") launched [an invasion of Joseon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_conquest_of_Gojoseon "Han conquest of Gojoseon"), conquering much of northern Korea as far east as the [Sea of Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_of_Japan "Sea of Japan") and as far south as the Han River. The Han established [four commanderies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Commanderies_of_Han "Four Commanderies of Han") to govern the area, although most were shortly lived; by 75 BCE, only the [Lelang Commandery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lelang_Commandery "Lelang Commandery") near modern Pyongyang remained in Chinese control. Although the Lelang Commandery dominated portions of North Korea for around 400 years, it left relatively few archaeological remains. Tombs and burial mounds are the most common archaeological sites from the Lelang period.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson1993165%E2%80%93169-31) Some dates are obtainable from Lelang artifacts, such as a [lacquer bowl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lacquerware "Lacquerware") dated to the year 69 CE.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson1993173-32)

From around 300 to 668, the Korean peninsula was mainly divided between three expansionist kingdoms: [Goguryeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goguryeo "Goguryeo") in the north, [Paekche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paekche "Paekche") in the southwest, and [Silla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silla "Silla") in the southeast. A fourth state, the [Kaya confederacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaya_confederacy "Kaya confederacy"), emerged along the [Nakdong River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nakdong_River "Nakdong River") on the southern coast. The most prominent archaeological features of the [Three Kingdoms Period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Kingdoms_of_Korea "Three Kingdoms of Korea") are the large elite tombs from each polity.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelsonNeu2017607-33)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson1993165%E2%80%93169-31) [Buddhism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism "Buddhism") was introduced to the peninsula during the late 300s and was adopted by each of the three kingdoms.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson1993221,_245-34)

Around the 1st century BCE, Goguryeo emerged in the Yalu River basin in what is now northeastern China.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelsonNeu2017607-33)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson1993165%E2%80%93169-31) The Lelang Commandery held onto a stretch of territory in northern Korea, but was bordered to the north by the expanding Goguryeo and by the [Samhan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samhan "Samhan") confederacies in the south. Frequent military conflicts between the Goguryeo and the Lelang Commandery are recorded from 12 CE onward. Chinese forces were unable to conquer the kingdom. The _Records of the Three Kingdoms_ records that Goguryeo conquered and extracted tribute from the [Okjeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okjeo "Okjeo") tribes in [Hamgyong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamgyong_Province "Hamgyong Province") before the late 3rd century. In 313, the Goguryeo conquered Lelang and began to push south against Paekche, establishing a frontier in the Han River basin.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelsonNeu2017608%E2%80%93612-35)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson1993206%E2%80%93211-36) At its greatest extent, around the beginning of the 5th century, the kingdom had conquered northwest as far as the [Liao River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liao_River "Liao River"). They established a new capital at Pyongyang in 427, although continued occupying their initial heartland along the Yalu.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson1993207,_211-37)

The Goguryeo developed a distinct material culture with influence both from China and from the nomadic groups of the northwest. [Goguryeo royal tombs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goguryeo_royal_tombs "Goguryeo royal tombs") initially took the form of pyramidal structures made of cut stone, while later examples are hemispherical [tumuli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tumulus "Tumulus") containing stone burial chambers. Although almost universally plundered in antiquity, many of them still contain elaborate murals. Horse equipment has been found at Goguryeo sites, including some of the earliest examples of [stirrups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stirrup "Stirrup").[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelsonNeu2017612%E2%80%93613-38)[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson1993211%E2%80%93217-39)

The state of Silla enjoyed relative isolation in the southeast of the peninsula, protected by natural barriers from Paekche, Goguryeo, and China.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson1993243-40) By the 500s, the expanding Silla state had reached as far north as [South Hamgyong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Hamgyong_Province "South Hamgyong Province") in northern Korea, testified by two stone markers installed on the orders of [King Jinheung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jinheung_of_Silla "Jinheung of Silla").[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson1993245-41) Allying with the [Tang dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tang_dynasty "Tang dynasty"), the Silla conquered Paekche in 660 and Goguryeo in 668, unifying much of the peninsula and beginning the [Unified Silla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unified_Silla "Unified Silla") period,[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson1993247-42) which would last until 935.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelsonNeu2017616-43) Portions of what is now northeast China, the Russian Far East, and North Korea became part of the [Parhae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balhae "Balhae") in 698, established in a revolt against Tang incursions by the Goguryeo people and the [Mohe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohe_people "Mohe people") tribes. Parhae would last until 926, when it was conquered by an alliance between Silla and the [Khitan Liao dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liao_dynasty "Liao dynasty").[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKim2011345%E2%80%93347,_354-44)

Archaeological studies
----------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archaeology_of_North_Korea&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Archaeological studies")\]

Korea did not have a systemic tradition of archaeology prior to its introduction into East Asia during the late 19th century. Antiquarian texts contained relatively cursory mentions of ancient structures and inscriptions, while interest towards prehistory and artifacts was relatively limited. Stone tools found in the region were often called 'thunder-axes' (雷斧, _noebu_) or 'thunder-daggers' (雷劒, _noegŏm_) by scholars during the [Joseon dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseon "Joseon") (1392–1897). The predominant early view considered them artifacts of the Chinese thunder god [Leigong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leigong "Leigong"), possibly containing magical or medicinal value. The 15th century scholar [Yi Yuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yi_Yuk&action=edit&redlink=1 "Yi Yuk (page does not exist)") ([ko](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EC%9D%B4%EC%9C%A1 "ko:이육")) wrote that they must have been shaped by an artisan, but could not understand how or why they were made. Writing in the early 19th century, the scholar [Kim Chŏnghŭi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Ch%C5%8Fngh%C5%ADi "Kim Chŏnghŭi") discovered stone arrowheads in the northeast of Korea; he identified them with the '[bush clover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bush_clover "Bush clover") arrows' of the [Sushen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sushen "Sushen"), a people of northeastern China mentioned in the Han dynasty chronicle _[Shiji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shiji "Shiji")_.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYi2002293%E2%80%93299-45)

[![Image 5: A black and white photo of an older man in a suit and glasses looking right](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/Sekino_1.jpg/250px-Sekino_1.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sekino_1.jpg)

[Sekino Tadashi](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sekino_Tadashi&action=edit&redlink=1 "Sekino Tadashi (page does not exist)") ([ja](https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%96%A2%E9%87%8E%E8%B2%9E "ja:関野貞")), a Japanese scholar who conducted early archaeological surveys of Korea

Modern archaeology began in Korea during the [Korean Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Empire "Korean Empire") (1897–1910), when the country began to fall under Japanese influence. Archaeologists were strongly limited in their ability to conduct excavations in Japan, and so the early Japanese archaeological community began to investigate sites in other regions of East Asia.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson200638%E2%80%9341-46) Initial archaeological interest in Korea was spurred by a desire to find evidence of the ancestral [Yamato people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yamato_people "Yamato people"), which they believed had to come to Japan from the peninsula; Japanese nationalist theorists believed Koreans and Japanese [to descend from a common ancestor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nissen_d%C5%8Dsoron "Nissen dōsoron").[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPai2013112%E2%80%93114-47) Most early investigations were surveys conducted by the [Tokyo Imperial University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Tokyo "University of Tokyo"). In 1900, the Tokyo Imperial University anthropologist [Tsuboi Shōgorō](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Tsuboi_Sh%C5%8Dgor%C5%8D&action=edit&redlink=1 "Tsuboi Shōgorō (page does not exist)") ([ja](https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%9D%AA%E4%BA%95%E6%AD%A3%E4%BA%94%E9%83%8E "ja:坪井正五郎")) dispatched his student [Yagi Sōzaburō](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Yagi_S%C5%8Dzabur%C5%8D&action=edit&redlink=1 "Yagi Sōzaburō (page does not exist)") ([ja](https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E5%85%AB%E6%9C%A8%E5%A5%98%E4%B8%89%E9%83%8E "ja:八木奘三郎")) to Korea to conduct the first archaeological survey of the country. Yagi's survey lasted four months and covered prehistoric and historic sites across Korea, including in the area around Pyongyang.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPak2018404-48)

Two years later, the Japanese scholar [Sekino Tadashi](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sekino_Tadashi&action=edit&redlink=1 "Sekino Tadashi (page does not exist)") ([ja](https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%96%A2%E9%87%8E%E8%B2%9E "ja:関野貞")) conducted a survey of art and archaeological history around four former royal capitals, including Pyongyang (the capital of Gojoseon and Goguryeo) and Kaesong (the capital of Goryeo). Sekino's research was compiled into a report published in 1904, _Investigator's Report of Korean Architecture_, which featured a periodization scheme of Korean art history and photographs of various temples, tombs, and ruins, informing the broader academic world of the presence of such archaeological sites in the peninsula.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPai2013139-49) During the 1900s, Japanese antique dealers and looters began to plunder archaeological sites in Korea; the [Royal Tombs of the Goryeo Dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Tombs_of_the_Goryeo_Dynasty "Royal Tombs of the Goryeo Dynasty") around Kaesong were especially hard-hit, as they were poorly protected and contained valuable grave goods such as the [Goryeo celadon ware](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goryeo_ware "Goryeo ware").[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPak2018405-50)

At the request of the [Japanese Residency-General of Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Japanese_Residency-General_of_Korea&action=edit&redlink=1 "Japanese Residency-General of Korea (page does not exist)") ([ja](https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E7%B5%B1%E7%9B%A3%E5%BA%9C "ja:統監府"); [ko](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%ED%86%B5%EA%B0%90%EB%B6%80 "ko:통감부")) (and later [Government-General of Chōsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government-General_of_Ch%C5%8Dsen "Government-General of Chōsen") ([ja](https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E6%9C%9D%E9%AE%AE%E7%B7%8F%E7%9D%A3%E5%BA%9C "ja:朝鮮総督府"); [ko](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EC%A1%B0%EC%84%A0%EC%B4%9D%EB%8F%85%EB%B6%80 "ko:조선총독부")), GGC), Sekino and [Torii Ryūzō](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torii_Ry%C5%ABz%C5%8D "Torii Ryūzō") conducted large-scale systemic surveys of archaeological sites in Korea. Sekino's survey, made from 1909 to 1911, primarily focused on architecture and relics,[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPak2018405-50) while Torii's 1910–1911 survey was intended to supplement it with anthropological and ethnographic information. Taking place during the official [annexation of Korea by Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan%E2%80%93Korea_Treaty_of_1910 "Japan–Korea Treaty of 1910") in 1910, these surveys were intended to support colonial rule; confirming the presence of the ancient Lelang Commandery around Pyongyang was seen as a way to legitimize Japanese rule. Sekino's survey produced an inventory of 579 historical sites, sorted into four ranks by priority of preservation. Over the course of the survey, Sekino and his team excavated various tombs, and brought most of the discovered materials to Japan.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPak2018406-51) Japanese archaeologists did not generally train Korean students; only a few amateur archaeologists assisted Japanese teams.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson200638%E2%80%9341-46)

A group of people in white caps stand in the foreground, carrying large vases above their head](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/Taedong-gun_Lelang_Tomb_2_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Taedong-gun_Lelang_Tomb_2_%28cropped%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Taedong-gun_Lelang_Tomb_2_/(cropped/).jpg)

Japanese archaeologists standing atop [Taedong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taedong_County "Taedong County") Lelang Tomb 2, near Pyongyang, 1915

In 1916, the GGC promulgated a set of regulations governing archaeological remains in Korea, and established the Commission for the Investigation of Ancient Sites to explore archaeological sites on the peninsula. The commission set a five-year plan for surveying sites: in the first year (1916), they examined sites from Goguryeo and the Four Commanderies of Han; in the second, Samhan, Gaya, and Baekje; in the third, Silla and prehistoric sites; in the fourth, Silla, Yemaek, Okjeo, and Balhae; and in the fifth, two sites in the south. The commission was superseded by the Department of Investigation of Ancient Sites in 1921, founded to consolidate archaeological research in colonial Korea, while the following year the GGC established the [Korean History Compilation Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_History_Compilation_Committee "Korean History Compilation Committee").[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPak2018407%E2%80%93408-52) A major focus of the compilation was to testify to the influence of the Han commanderies in the north, as well as to the existence of a purported ancient Japanese colony called [Mimana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mimana "Mimana") in the south.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPak2018409-53)

In the wake of the [Great Depression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Depression "Great Depression") and the [Japanese invasion of Manchuria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japanese_invasion_of_Manchuria "Japanese invasion of Manchuria"), state financial support for archaeological research declined during the 1930s. To make up for this, Japanese archaeologist [Katsumi Kuroita](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Katsumi_Kuroita&action=edit&redlink=1 "Katsumi Kuroita (page does not exist)") ([ja](https://ja.wikipedia.org/wiki/%E9%BB%92%E6%9D%BF%E5%8B%9D%E7%BE%8E "ja:黒板勝美"); [ko](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EA%B5%AC%EB%A1%9C%EC%9D%B4%ED%83%80_%EA%B0%80%EC%93%B0%EB%AF%B8 "ko:구로이타 가쓰미")) created the Society for the Research of Korean Ancient Sites, financed by private and state donations from organizations such as the [Ministry of the Imperial Household](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ministry_of_the_Imperial_Household "Ministry of the Imperial Household") and the [Prince Yi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yi_Un "Yi Un") Family Household. The society established offices in [Gyeongju](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gyeongju "Gyeongju"), [Buyeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buyeo_County "Buyeo County"), and Pyongyang. The society also established [Kaesong Municipal Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kaesong_Municipal_Museum&action=edit&redlink=1 "Kaesong Municipal Museum (page does not exist)") in 1931 and the [Pyongyang Municipal Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Pyongyang_Municipal_Museum&action=edit&redlink=1 "Pyongyang Municipal Museum (page does not exist)") in 1933. That same year, the GGC established the Chōsen Sōtokufu Committee for the Preservation of Korean Treasures, Ancient Remains, Famous Places, and Natural Monuments in an attempt to curb the illicit antiquities trade. In 1933, the committee established a revamped set of heritage protections, stronger than the 1916 rules.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPak2018410%E2%80%93411-54)

[![Image 7: An ancient mural, slightly faded, showing a procession of soldiers and men on horseback](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Dongshouprocessionmural.jpg/250px-Dongshouprocessionmural.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Dongshouprocessionmural.jpg)

Mural in [Anak Tomb No. 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anak_Tomb_No._3 "Anak Tomb No. 3"), discovered in 1949 as one of the first major archaeological discoveries of the independent North Korea

In 1945, following the defeat of Japan in [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), Korea was partitioned into [Soviet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Civil_Administration "Soviet Civil Administration") and [American occupation zones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Military_Government_in_Korea "United States Army Military Government in Korea"). This was initially intended as a temporary measure. The two zones became the [Democratic People's Republic of Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_People%27s_Republic_of_Korea "Democratic People's Republic of Korea") (North Korea) and [Republic of Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Korea "Republic of Korea") (South Korea), both claiming to be the legitimate government of the region.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson200642-55) In 1946, the [Provisional People's Committee of North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provisional_People%27s_Committee_of_North_Korea "Provisional People's Committee of North Korea") (an early iteration of the North Korean government) instituted a slate of cultural and heritage protections. [To Yu-ho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/To_Yu-ho "To Yu-ho"), an archaeologist educated abroad in Germany and Austria during the 1930s, emerged from hiding after 1945 and was hired as an archaeology professor at the National University of Pyongyang (now [Kim Il Sung University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Il_Sung_University "Kim Il Sung University")) in 1946. He was joined there by another European-educated archaeologist, [Han Hŭng-su](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Han_H%C5%ADng-su&action=edit&redlink=1 "Han Hŭng-su (page does not exist)"), in 1948; together, To and Han emerged as the founding figures of archaeology in the newly independent state.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYoo2016279%E2%80%93281-56)

Academia in early North Korea was largely based off the Soviet Union, and its archaeology was largely based off [Soviet archaeology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_the_Soviet_Union "Archaeology of the Soviet Union"), which heavily featured [Marxist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marxism "Marxism") elements.[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee2013404%E2%80%93405-57) Among the first major archaeological discoveries of the newly independent North Korea was the excavation of a shell midden in [Unggi County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unggi_County "Unggi County") in 1947 and the discovery of three [Goguryeo tombs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goguryeo_tombs "Goguryeo tombs") (including the richly-decorated [Anak Tomb No. 3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anak_Tomb_No._3 "Anak Tomb No. 3")) in 1949 near Pyongyang.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYoo2016281%E2%80%93282-58) Initial articles were included in the ethnographic journal _[Munhwa yumul](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Munhwa_yumul&action=edit&redlink=1 "Munhwa yumul (page does not exist)")_, which was published from 1949 to 1950, and afterwards in various historical journals.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee2013405-59)

The [Korean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War "Korean War") broke out in 1950 after North Korean forces invaded the south. After three years of fighting, an armistice was signed, dividing Korea along the [Military Demarcation Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_Demarcation_Line "Military Demarcation Line").[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson200642-55) While archaeological excavations were paused during the war, the war years saw the foundation of the [Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Sciences_of_the_Democratic_People%27s_Republic_of_Korea "Academy of Sciences of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea") in 1952, including the Institute of Material Culture (IMC) headed by To. Around the same time, Han was purged from academic influence for unclear reasons, possibly stemming from criticism by To. This left To as the dominant force in domestic archaeology.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYoo2016281%E2%80%93282-58)

Archaeological excavations resumed in 1954, following the armistice, with early archaeological work aimed at documenting and restoring cultural heritage damaged during the war. Led by To, North Korean archaeologists excavated a number of important archaeological sites during the 1950s, including the Bronze Age [Odong site](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Odong_site&action=edit&redlink=1 "Odong site (page does not exist)") in [Hoeryong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoeryong "Hoeryong") (1954–1955) and the Neolithic [Jitapri site](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jitapri_site&action=edit&redlink=1 "Jitapri site (page does not exist)") in [Pongsan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pongsan_County "Pongsan County") (1957).[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYoo2016281%E2%80%93282-58) During the 1950s and early 1960s, there were about twenty active archaeologists in North Korea, most with no prior academic experience.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee2013402-60) They conducted about 128 field investigations during the 1950s, significantly more than their South Korean counterparts. The first archaeology-specific journal_, Munhwa yusan_ ('Cultural Heritage'), was published in 1957 by the Institute of Archaeology and Ethnography (formerly the IMC).[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee2013405,_410-61)

Although To was politically powerful and a loyal member of the ruling [Workers' Party of Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Workers%27_Party_of_Korea "Workers' Party of Korea"), his support of [cultural diffusionism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_diffusion "Cultural diffusion") brought him in conflict with Marxist orthodoxy, which favored [historical materialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_materialism "Historical materialism") and theories of autochthonic development. To's theories of cultural diffusion incorporated highly criticized hypotheses; he theorized that [megaliths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megalith "Megalith") had emerged from the tradition of Ancient Egyptian [mastabas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mastaba "Mastaba"), which spread to Korea via [Indochina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indochina "Indochina").[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYoo2016283%E2%80%93285-62) By the late 1950s, North Korean archaeologists had generally adopted the [culture-historical model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture-historical_archaeology "Culture-historical archaeology") in favor of historical materialism; To wrote that the turn towards the model was necessary in order to promote the national cultural heritage.[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee2013412-63) In 1963, archaeologists discovered [Paleolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleolithic "Paleolithic") lithic artifacts at the Gulpori site, the first known Paleolithic site in Korea. This was hailed as a major breakthrough in the nation's archaeology.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee2013416-64)

Around 1965, academic conditions in North Korea rapidly changed. To's culture-historical model fell out of support, as it was seen as contrary to the increasingly promoted ideas of [socialist patriotism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_patriotism "Socialist patriotism"). The supreme leader [Kim Il Sung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Il_Sung "Kim Il Sung") increasingly criticized academics, seeing them as too influenced by bourgeois thought; To was purged in 1965 and removed from influence, while almost all academic work was halted by 1967, including archaeology. Academia would slowly reemerge during the 1970s in a condition strongly influenced by _[Juche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juche "Juche")_, the emerging state ideology.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee2013416%E2%80%93417-65)[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYoo2016288%E2%80%93289-66)

> Our country boasts a long history, a history that began with the very first phase of mankind. Our Palaeolithic sites and artifacts clearly address that our ancestors have permanently resided in this land. Their gifted creativity enabled themselves to conquer the nature, to succeed in social evolution and to enjoy cultural prosperity.

_Palaeolithic Sites of Northern Korea_, Institute of Archaeology of the Academy of Social Sciences, 2009[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYoo2016289-67)

From the 1980s to the 2010s, [Seo Guktae](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Seo_Guktae&action=edit&redlink=1 "Seo Guktae (page does not exist)") (a Neolithic and Bronze Age specialist) and [Jang Woojin](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jang_Woojin_\(archaeologist\)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Jang Woojin (archaeologist) (page does not exist)") (a [human evolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_evolution "Human evolution") researcher) have been two of the most prolific and influential archaeologists in North Korea. Other prominent modern archaeologists include [Kim Incheol](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kim_Incheol&action=edit&redlink=1 "Kim Incheol (page does not exist)") (writing on Goguryeo, Goryeo, and Balhae) and [Choi Seungtaek](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Choi_Seungtaek&action=edit&redlink=1 "Choi Seungtaek (page does not exist)"), the most prolific Goguryeo archaeologist.[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKo202363%E2%80%9366-68)

Ideology and perspectives
-------------------------

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Archaeology_of_North_Korea&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Ideology and perspectives")\]

Modern North Korean archaeology has oriented itself towards the state ideology of Juche. Excavations are prioritized as a means to study the ancient past of the Korean people. Archaeological papers frequently contain nationalist elements and praise for the nation and the Korean people.[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYoo2016288%E2%80%93289-66) According to Juche thought, the Korean people form a single ethnicity and bloodline,[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTELeeKim2024104-69) and Korean civilization developed without outside influence. North Korean archaeological thought sees the spread of bronze metallurgy as a purely indigenous development, and the Commandaries of Han are identified as a local kingdom. North Korean scholars view Korean cultural influence as traditionally extending to a large portion of Northeastern China, which they believe was conquered by Gojoseon and Goguryeo. In keeping with traditional Marxist historiography, Gojoseon is seen as a [slave society](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Slave_society&action=edit&redlink=1 "Slave society (page does not exist)"), while the Three Kingdoms are analogous to [feudal society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudal_society "Feudal society").[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson199937-70)

North Korean archaeologists have been less reliant on [radiocarbon dating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radiocarbon_dating "Radiocarbon dating") than their southern counterparts, eschewing it due to expense or in favor of gathering dates from historical records and traditional accounts. As a result, South Korean archaeological chronology is more conservative than in the north,[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson200649-71) with later dates given for the Neolithic, Bronze Age, and the founding of Gojoseon. The Bronze Age is considered to have begun c. 2000 BCE in North Korea, while South Korean archaeologists estimate it around a millennium or more later.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTENelson199937-70)

[![Image 8: A marble pyramid mausoleum with a lion statue](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/Laika_ac_Mausoleum_of_Tangun_%287987312460%29.jpg/250px-Laika_ac_Mausoleum_of_Tangun_%287987312460%29.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Laika_ac_Mausoleum_of_Tangun_/(7987312460/).jpg)

The modern [Mausoleum of Tangun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mausoleum_of_Tangun "Mausoleum of Tangun"), the mythical founder of [Gojoseon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Chos%C5%8Fn "Old Chosŏn"), built at the site of his purported tomb

Following the work of the historian [Ri Chirin](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ri_Chirin&action=edit&redlink=1 "Ri Chirin (page does not exist)") during the 1960s, North Korean scholars generally regard the story of [Gija](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jizi "Jizi"), a semi-legendary [Shang dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shang_dynasty "Shang dynasty") noble who allegedly journeyed east and founded [Gija Joseon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gija_Joseon "Gija Joseon") around the 11th century BCE, as a later Chinese fabrication. In contrast, some South Korean historians interpret his migration as a historical event.[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEShim2002280-72) However, North Korean archaeologists have been more sympathetic to the historicity of the legendary king and deity [Dangun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dangun "Dangun"), said to have founded Gojoseon in 2333 BCE. In 1994, archaeologists found a pyramidal tomb with several enclosed skeletons near Pyongyang; the North Korean government announced that it had found the [Tomb of Tangun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mausoleum_of_Tangun "Mausoleum of Tangun"), and that its discovery "demonstrated" the ancient origins of the Korean people. Although the tomb resembled Goguryeo-era tombs, this was suggested to be the result of later repairs.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYoo2016290-73)[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGrayson2015262-74)

Institutions and publications
-----------------------------

A tower block and a North Korean flag are in the distance.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9a/Kim_Il-Sung_University.jpg/250px-Kim_Il-Sung_University.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kim_Il-Sung_University.jpg)

[Kim Il Sung University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Il_Sung_University "Kim Il Sung University") in Pyongyang offers degrees in archaeology and maintains an archaeology journal.

The Institute of Archaeology of the [Academy of Social Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Academy_of_Social_Sciences_\(North_Korea\)&action=edit&redlink=1 "Academy of Social Sciences (North Korea) (page does not exist)") ([ko](https://ko.wikipedia.org/wiki/%EC%82%AC%ED%9A%8C%EA%B3%BC%ED%95%99%EC%9B%90 "ko:사회과학원")) and the Faculty of History at [Kim Il Sung University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Il_Sung_University "Kim Il Sung University") both offer degrees in archaeology, carry out research excavations, and publish their own [academic journals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_journal "Academic journal").[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKo202377%E2%80%9378-75) Researchers at the [Joseon Folk Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Joseon_Folk_Museum&action=edit&redlink=1 "Joseon Folk Museum (page does not exist)"), [Korean Central History Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_Central_History_Museum "Korean Central History Museum"), [Cultural Preservation Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Cultural_Preservation_Institute&action=edit&redlink=1 "Cultural Preservation Institute (page does not exist)"), and [University of Construction and Building Materials](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Construction_and_Building_Materials&action=edit&redlink=1 "University of Construction and Building Materials (page does not exist)") have also been known to publish archaeological research articles.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKo202371-76) The Academy of Social Sciences also publishes research [monographs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monograph "Monograph").[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEYoo2016288%E2%80%93289-66)

The first North Korean archaeological journal was _Munhwa yusan_ ('Cultural Heritage'), published in Pyongyang from 1957 to 1962. The following year, it was superseded by another journal, _Kogo minsok_ ('Archaeology and Ethnography').[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTELee2013405,_410-61) _[Joseon gogo yeongu](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Joseon_gogo_yeongu&action=edit&redlink=1 "Joseon gogo yeongu (page does not exist)")_ ('Korean Archaeological Research') is now the primary North Korean academic journal covering archaeology, published uninterrupted by the Institute of Archaeology since 1986. It featured 1,656 articles between its initial issue and 2019, not including its annual indices. Most articles within the journal are research articles, although excavation and site reports, alongside smaller numbers of transcribed lectures, [data sets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_set "Data set"), news articles, and pieces of political rhetoric. Political pieces in _Joseon gogo yeongu_ are relatively infrequent in comparison to those in the _[Ryeoksa gwahak](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ryeoksa_gwahak&action=edit&redlink=1 "Ryeoksa gwahak (page does not exist)")_ ('Historical Science'), a history journal published by the Academy of Social Sciences which also occasionally includes archaeological research.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKo202361%E2%80%9368-77)

The Faculty of History at Kim Il Sung University also maintains its own journal, _Kim Il Seong jonghap daehak hakbo—ryeoksa-beomnyul/ryeoksahak_ ('Journal of Kim Il Sung University—History-Law/History'), which contains articles on archaeology alongside other history topics. While archaeologists at Kim Il Sung University often publish in the _Joseon gogo yeongu_, it is unknown if archaeologists from other universities can publish in the _Kil Il Seong jonghap daehak hakbo_.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKo202377%E2%80%9378-75) Archaeology articles are also found within a variety of other North Korean academic journals, including _Minjok munhwa yusan_ ('Our People's Cultural Heritage'), _Ryeoksa jemunje_ ('Questions of History'), and _Joseon geonchuk_ ('Joseon Architecture').[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeology_of_North_Korea#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKo202358%E2%80%9359-78)
